summaries.example: Imagine two paintings made with exactly the same tiny arrangements of paint. They must have the same shapes and colors on the canvas. If one painting had a different shape or color arrangement, some tiny physical detail would also be different. The shapes and colors therefore supervene on the tiny physical details. Other features, such as which painting was made by a famous artist, may be different even when the physical details are the same.
summaries.summary: Supervenience is a philosophical idea about patterns of difference. A group of properties A supervenes on a group B when two things cannot differ in their A-properties without also differing in their B-properties. Another way to say this is that being exactly alike in B guarantees being exactly alike in A. The connection may be understood as necessary in different ways. It might be required by logic, by the nature of reality, or only by the laws of nature. Philosophers distinguish several versions, including weak and strong forms, forms about individuals and whole possible worlds, and forms based on similarity rather than exact sameness. Supervenience is useful, but it says less than some stronger ideas. By itself, it does not tell us why the connection exists, whether one feature is reduced to another, or whether one thing is grounded in another. The term is a special philosophy word, even though an older everyday use of “supervene” means that something comes later or unexpectedly.
key_ideas: Supervenience means that one kind of difference requires another kind of difference.
The word “cannot” is important: the connection is meant to hold beyond what merely happens by chance.
Some properties may supervene on physical properties, but philosophers disagree about exactly how strong the connection is.
Supervenience is not automatically the same as explanation, reduction, or dependence.
Philosophers use supervenience to discuss minds, morals, art, physicalism, and objects made from other objects.
summaries.why_it_matters: Supervenience gives philosophers a careful way to ask whether one kind of fact is fixed by another kind. It can help compare claims about the physical world and the mind, or about physical details and artistic or moral features. It also helps test proposed explanations: if a theory says one kind of feature can be reduced to another, the first feature should supervene on the second. But philosophers must ask for more than a pattern of matching differences when they want a full explanation.

important_terms.definition: A relationship in which there cannot be a difference in one group of properties without a difference in another group.
A feature something has, such as its color, size, value, or shape.
The features of something at the very small physical level, such as the arrangement of its parts.
A way things could be, used by philosophers to compare what might happen in different situations.

questions_to_think_about: If two things are exactly alike in every physical detail, must they be alike in every other way?
Could two paintings have the same colors and shapes but different histories?
Does saying that one feature supervenes on another explain why the connection holds?
What kinds of features seem to depend on a thing’s surroundings rather than only on the thing itself?

summaries.example: Suppose two possible situations contain individuals with exactly the same physical features, but one individual is conscious and the other has no conscious experience. If such a pair is metaphysically possible, then mental properties do not strongly metaphysically supervene on physical properties. If the pair is ruled out only by the laws of nature, mental properties may still supervene nomologically on physical properties. This illustrates why debates about consciousness often concern not whether there is some physical connection, but what kind of necessity the connection has.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry presents supervenience as a family of relations captured by the principle that there cannot be an A-difference without a B-difference. A supervenes on B when B-indiscernibility guarantees A-indiscernibility, with the guarantee evaluated over a selected range of possibilities. The range determines the modal force: a relation may hold with metaphysical necessity or only with nomological necessity. This distinction matters in philosophy of mind, where many philosophers accept a physical-to-mental connection but disagree about whether physically identical individuals could differ mentally in a metaphysically possible situation. The entry distinguishes weak and strong individual supervenience, regional and global forms, similarity-based supervenience, and multiple-domain versions. Strong individual supervenience entails strong global supervenience, but the converse can fail in cases involving extrinsic properties; under certain restrictions, especially for intrinsic properties or suitably closed property sets, several forms become equivalent. Supervenience resembles entailment because it is reflexive and transitive, yet it is not generally entailment. It is also distinct from reduction, grounding, ontological dependence, realization, and emergence. A supervenience claim records a pattern of covariation; it does not by itself explain the pattern. This limitation affects arguments about physicalism, internalism and externalism, haecceitism, and coincident objects.
key_ideas: The core claim is modal: it says that an A-difference cannot occur without a B-difference, not merely that no such difference happens in the actual world.
Supervenience can have different modal strengths, especially metaphysical and nomological necessity.
Strong supervenience is generally stronger than weak supervenience because it compares individuals across worlds as well as within a single world.
Global supervenience concerns world-wide patterns and can differ from individual supervenience, especially when extrinsic or relational properties are involved.
Supervenience has logical similarities to entailment, such as reflexivity and transitivity, but neither relation generally guarantees the other.
Supervenience by itself is not an explanation and does not automatically establish reduction, grounding, or ontological dependence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Supervenience functions as both a metaphysical thesis and an argumentative test. If a proposed reduction or conceptual analysis requires A to supervene on B, a possible counterexample involving B-similar but A-different cases threatens that proposal. The idea also clarifies debates about whether mental, moral, aesthetic, or modal facts are fixed by physical or non-modal facts. At the same time, the entry warns against treating supervenience as a complete theory: a necessary correlation may lack an explanation and may not show grounding, dependence, or reduction. Precisely identifying the type of supervenience and its modal force is therefore essential.

important_terms.definition: A relation in which no A-difference can occur without a B-difference; equivalently, exact B-similarity guarantees exact A-similarity.
A necessity that holds in every logically or metaphysically possible situation, according to the modal framework being used.
A necessity imposed by the laws of nature, even if other laws might have been possible.
A relation between sets of properties within one world: B-indiscernible individuals are also A-indiscernible in that world.
A relation requiring B-indiscernibility across different possible worlds to guarantee A-indiscernibility.
Supervenience concerning the overall distribution of properties across complete possible worlds rather than just particular individuals.
A relation in which one fact holds in virtue of another; supervenience alone does not entail this relation.
A philosophical claim that some properties or facts are nothing over and above others in a relevant ontological sense; whether supervenience establishes this is disputed.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a philosopher accept nomological supervenience of the mental on the physical while rejecting metaphysical supervenience?
Why can a property set supervene on another set without any single base property entailing the supervening property?
When might global supervenience be more useful than individual supervenience?
What would explain a supervenience claim rather than merely restate it?
Does metaphysically necessary supervenience show that supervening properties are not an additional ontological commitment?

summaries.example: Think about two game characters in two different game worlds. Suppose their physical game data is exactly alike, but one character is said to be brave and the other is not. A philosopher who believes bravery strongly supervenes on physical data would say that this situation cannot occur if the data are truly identical. A philosopher who accepts only a weaker claim might say that within any one game world, identical data always go with the same bravery status, while allowing a difference between separate possible worlds. The example shows why philosophers ask what “cannot” means and whether the comparison stays within one world or crosses between worlds.
summaries.summary: Supervenience is a technical idea used to describe one-way patterns of dependence between properties. If A-properties supervene on B-properties, then two things cannot differ in their A-properties while matching exactly in their B-properties. The claim is modal: it concerns what is impossible, not merely what happens in the actual world. Different claims can use different kinds of necessity, such as metaphysical necessity or necessity based on the laws of nature. Philosophers also distinguish weak and strong individual supervenience. Weak supervenience concerns matching individuals in the same possible world; strong supervenience compares individuals across possible worlds too. Global supervenience instead concerns whether whole worlds with the same B-pattern must have the same A-pattern. Other versions focus on regions, degrees of similarity, or properties possessed by related objects. The entry explains that supervenience resembles entailment in some formal respects, but it does not generally amount to entailment. Nor does it by itself prove that A reduces to B, that A is grounded in B, or that A depends for its existence on B. A supervenience statement identifies a pattern, while a further theory must explain why that pattern holds.
key_ideas: Supervenience says more than “these features usually occur together.” It says that a certain difference is impossible without another difference.
Weak supervenience compares individuals within one possible world; strong supervenience also compares individuals in different worlds.
Global supervenience compares the overall arrangement of properties in entire worlds.
A relation can be necessary because of logic or metaphysics, or necessary only because of natural laws.
Supervenience is related to reduction and grounding, but it is not automatically the same as either one.
Philosophers use supervenience to frame disagreements about the mind, morality, art, physicalism, and whether properties depend on surroundings.
summaries.why_it_matters: Supervenience helps philosophers make broad claims precise. For instance, someone might argue that mental facts are fixed by physical facts, or that moral differences require nonmoral differences. The exact version matters: a weak global claim could allow properties to be distributed among different individuals even when the overall pattern stays the same, while a strong version rules out that kind of swapping. Supervenience can also be used to challenge a proposed reduction: if a possible case has the same base features but a different higher-level feature, the reduction is in trouble. Still, showing supervenience is only a beginning, because it may not provide the deeper explanation a view

important_terms.definition: A rule-like connection in which a difference in one group of features requires a difference in another group.
A feature or way something is, such as being red, conscious, valuable, or heavy.
Having exactly the same features from a selected group of properties.
A way the world could have been, used to compare different possibilities.
A type of necessity connected with the laws of nature.
A type of necessity that holds across all metaphysically possible situations in the relevant philosophical theory.
Supervenience involving the complete pattern of properties across a whole possible world.
A relation in which something is the case because of, or in virtue of, something else; supervenience alone does not guarantee it.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between “has always happened” and “could not happen otherwise”?
Why might a feature depend on the environment around an object?
Can one feature supervene on another without the second feature explaining the first?
Why would a philosopher distinguish weak from strong supervenience?
Could two objects occupy the same place while having different nonphysical features?
